claim: Atherosclerosis preferentially occurs in atheroprone vasculature where human umbilical vein endothelial cells are exposed to disturbed flow.
source: Atherosclerosis preferentially occurs in atheroprone vasculature where human umbilical vein endothelial cells are exposed to disturbed flow.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about atherosclerosis and disturbed flow.

claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most prevalent internal modification of eukaryotic mRNA.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most prevalent internal modiﬁcation of eukaryotic mRNA
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Roundtree et al., 2017 in the Introduction section.

claim: Oscillatory stress (OS) reduced the expression of methyltransferase like 3 (METTL3), the primary m6A methyltransferase.
source: Oscillatory stress (OS) reduced the expression of methyltransferase like 3 (METTL3), the primary m6A methyltransferase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-E and western blot analysis described in the Results section.

claim: m6A modification of the EGFR 3' untranslated regions (3'UTR) accelerated its mRNA degradation.
source: m6A modification of the EGFR 3' untranslated regions (3'UTR) accelerated its mRNA degradation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from actinomycin D treatment experiments shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: Double mutation of the EGFR 3'UTR abolished METTL3-induced luciferase activity.
source: Double mutation of the EGFR 3'UTR abolished METTL3-induced luciferase activity.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated METTL3 overexpression significantly reduced EGFR activation and endothelial dysfunction in the presence of OS.
source: Adenovirus-mediated METTL3 overexpression significantly reduced EGFR activation and endothelial dysfunction in the presence of OS.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and immunofluorescence data in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) was specifically expressed in atheroprone regions without being affected by METTL3.
source: Furthermore, thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1), an EGFR ligand, was specifically expressed in atheroprone regions without being affected by METTL3.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of the TSP-1/EGFR axis by using shRNA and AG1478 significantly ameliorated atherogenesis.
source: Inhibition of the TSP-1/EGFR axis by using shRNA and AG1478 significantly ameliorated atherogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by lesion area quantification data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: OS significantly decreased m6A modification in HUVECs.
source: The results showed that OS significantly decreased m6A modification in HUVECs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by UHPLC-MRM-MS analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Western blot analysis detected a significantly decrease of METTL3 and Virillizer after OS stimulation, without affecting other m6A modulators.
source: Western blot analysis detected a significantly decrease of METTL3 and Virillizer after OS stimulation, without affecting other m6A modulators (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: METTL3 and Virilizer were significantly decreased in AA tissue lysates than in TA region, whereas METTL14 and WTAP were not changed.
source: Furthermore, to analyze the m6A modulators in atheroprone (aortic arch [AA]) and atheroprotective (thoracic aorta [TA]) regions, we performed western blot analysis and found that METTL3 and Virilizer were significantly decreased in AA tissue lysates than in TA region, whereas METTL14 and WTAP were not changed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: In the inner curvature and bifurcation of AA, where blood flow is disturbed, METTL3 was dramatically decreased.
source: Conversely, in the inner curvature and bifurcation of AA, where blood flow is disturbed, METTL3 was dramatically decreased (Figure 1F and G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: METTL3 was weakly expressed in LCA after 1 and 2 weeks compared with RCA.
source: Consistent with the AA, as compared with right common carotid artery (RCA), METTL3 was weakly expressed in LCA after 1 and 2 weeks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The protein levels of METTL3 were decreased in AA intima tissue lysates compared to TA in Mettl3flox/flox mice.
source: The protein levels of METTL3 were decreased in AA intima tissue lysates compared to TA in Mettl3flox/flox mice.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The level of the EC activation marker VCAM-1 was significantly increased in AA intima tissue lysates compared to TA intima lysates in both Mettl3flox/flox mice and EC-Mettl3KO mice.
source: The level of the EC activation marker VCAM-1 was significantly increased in AA intima tissue lysates compared to TA intima lysates in both Mettl3flox/flox mice and EC-Mettl3KO mice (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: En face immunofluorescence staining of LCA revealed reduced protein levels of METTL3 and enhanced levels of VCAM-1 in EC-Mettl3KO mice compared to RCA 2 weeks after ligation.
source: En face immunofluorescence staining of LCA revealed reduced protein levels of METTL3 and enhanced levels of VCAM-1 in EC-Mettl3KO mice compared to RCA 2 weeks after ligation (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Overexpression of METTL3 in ECs by adeno-associated virus (AAV9-METTL3 OE) inhibited VCAM-1 expression induced by partial ligation in LCA endothelium.
source: Overexpression of METTL3 in ECs by adeno-associated virus (AAV9-METTL3 OE) inhibited VCAM-1 expression induced by partial ligation in LCA endothelium (Figure 2F and G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: 10,515 and 10,580 m6A peaks were identified in ST and OS, respectively, all of which were enriched in coding regions, 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs), and near stop codons.
source: We identified 10,515 and 10,580 m6A peaks in ST and OS, respectively, all of which were enriched in coding regions, 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs), and near stop codons (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The m6A motifs identified in OS and ST were significantly enriched in GGACU.
source: Interestingly, we found that the m6A motifs identified in OS and ST were significantly enriched in GGACU (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Genes with downregulated m6A peaks were significantly enriched in transcription regulation- and cell-cell and membrane adhesion-related pathways.
source: Furthermore, we identified thousands of dysregulated m6A peaks induced by OS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1), and genes with downregulated m6A peaks were significantly enriched in transcription regulation- and cell-cell and membrane adhesion-related pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 547 consistently upregulated genes were identified upon OS.
source: We identified 547 consistently upregulated genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F) upon OS.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: EGFR was identified as a potential key regulator participating in OS-enhanced gene ontology (GO) pathways.
source: According to the IPA analysis, we identified EGFR as a potential key regulator participating in OS-enhanced gene ontology (GO) pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is supported by IPA analysis of MeRIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The ratio of EGFR (IP/input) was reduced in OS compared to ST.
source: which was further confirmed by the reduced ratio of EGFR (IP/input) in OS compared to ST (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EGFR mRNA levels were significantly increased in OS compared to ST.
source: We also validated the significantly increased EGFR mRNA levels (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: m6A enrichment on EGFR mRNA was decreased in OS compared to ST.
source: and decreased m6A enrichment in OS compared to ST by MeRIP-quantitative PCR (qPCR) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by MeRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: METTL3 overexpression significantly decreased the remaining EGFR mRNA levels due to accelerated mRNA decay.
source: Compared to the green fluorescent protein (GFP) control, METTL3 overexpression significantly decreased the remaining EGFR mRNA levels due to accelerated mRNA decay in the presence of functional m6A modification by overexpression of METTL3 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by actinomycin D chase assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: EGFR mRNA showed a slower decay rate in response to METTL3 knockdown or OS treatment.
source: As expected, EGFR mRNA showed a slower decay rate in response to METTL3 knockdown or OS treatment (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by actinomycin D chase assay data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: The 3'UTR mutants did not respond to the decrease in luciferase activity caused by overexpression of METTL3.
source: Notably, the 3'UTR mutants did not respond to the decrease in luciferase activity caused by overexpression of METTL3 (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: Overexpression of METTL3 abolished phosphorylation of EGFR (Tyr-1068), AKT, and ERK, as well as total EGFR and VCAM-1 levels in response to OS.
source: Overexpression of METTL3 abolished phosphorylation of EGFR (Tyr-1068), AKT, and ERK, as well as total EGFR and VCAM-1 levels in response to OS (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: TSP-1 was significantly increased at both the mRNA and protein levels under OS.
source: Furthermore, TSP-1 was significantly increased at both the mRNA and protein levels under OS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Supplementation with recombinant human TSP-1 didn't change EGFR protein levels but enhanced EGFR phosphorylation which could be abolished by METTL3 overexpression.
source: Supplementation with recombinant human TSP-1 didn't change EGFR protein levels but enhanced EGFR phosphorylation which could be abolished by METTL3 overexpression (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: AG1478 blocked both OS and siMETTL3-mediated phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, and ERK and VCAM-1 levels, had no effect on total EGFR expression.
source: Next, ECs were subjected to OS or METTL3 siRNA in the presence of the EGFR-selective tyrphostin AG1478, which blocked both OS and siMETTL3-mediated phosphorylation of EGFR, AKT, and ERK and VCAM-1 levels, had no effect on total EGFR expression (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E-H.

claim: The increased number of THP-1 cells adhering to HUVECs by OS or siMETTL3 was relieved in the presence of overexpression of METTL3 or AG1478.
source: The increased number of THP-1 (human myeloid leukemia mononuclear) cells adhering to HUVECs by OS or siMETTL3 was relieved in the presence of overexpression of METTL3 or AG1478 (Figure 4F and H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is supported by cell adhesion assay data shown in Figure 4F and H.

claim: Overexpression of METTL3 inhibited EGFR expression induced by EC Mettl3 deficiency in partially ligated carotid artery but had no effect on TSP-1 levels with partial ligation.
source: Overexpression of METTL3 inhibited EGFR expression induced by EC Mettl3 deficiency in partially ligated carotid artery but had no effect on TSP-1 levels with partial ligation (Figure 5A–D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The lesion areas in the ligated carotid artery were more serious in Apoe-/- EC-Mettl3KO mice than in Apoe-/- Mettl3flox/flox mice at both 2 and 4 weeks.
source: The lesion areas in the ligated carotid artery were more serious in Apoe-/- EC-Mettl3KO mice than in Apoe-/- Mettl3flox/flox mice at both 2 and 4 weeks (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by lesion area quantification data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The levels of plasma triglyceride and cholesterol and body weight did not change among the groups.
source: The levels of plasma triglyceride and cholesterol and body weight did not change among the groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by plasma lipid and body weight measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: In comparison with Apoe-/- Mettl3flox/flox mice, Mettl3-deficient ECs significantly increased the total and AA atherosclerotic area in aortas.
source: Oil Red O staining of aortas revealed that, in comparison with Apoe-/- Mettl3flox/flox mice, Mettl3-deficient ECs significantly increased the total and AA atherosclerotic area in aortas (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Mettl3 deficiency increased the lesion area, lipid deposition, and macrophage infiltration, as well as EGFR and VCAM-1 expression, but had minimal effects on collagen fiber or vascular smooth muscle cell content.
source: Aortic root staining showed that Mettl3 deficiency increased the lesion area, lipid deposition, and macrophage infiltration, as well as EGFR and VCAM-1 expression, but had minimal effects on collagen fiber or vascular smooth muscle cell content (Figure 6C–H).
evidence: This is supported by histological staining and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C-H.

claim: The lesion area in Apoe-/- EC-Mettl3KO mice was significantly increased by 2.5-fold compared to that in Apoe-/- Mettl3flox/flox mice two weeks after ligation.
source: Two weeks after ligation, the lesion area in Apoe-/- EC-Mettl3KO mice was significantly increased by 2.5-fold compared to that in Apoe-/- Mettl3flox/flox mice.
evidence: This is supported by lesion area quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Thbs1 knockdown successfully reversed the lesion area in both genotypes of mice.
source: However, Thbs1 knockdown successfully reversed the lesion area in both genotypes of mice (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by lesion area quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: AG1478 significantly reduced the phosphorylation of EGFR without affecting the total EGFR levels in both genotypes of mice.
source: The EGFR-selective tyrphostin AG1478 significantly reduced the phosphorylation of EGFR without affecting the total EGFR levels in both genotypes of mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: AG1478 exerted the same anti-atherosclerotic effect as Thbs1 knockdown.
source: Consistent with Thbs1 knockdown, AG1478 exerted the same anti-atherosclerotic effect (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by lesion area quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Both Thbs1 knockdown and AG1478 inhibited the expression of VCAM-1 induced by EC Mettl3 deficiency in partially ligated carotid artery.
source: Both of them inhibited the expression of VCAM-1 induced by EC Mettl3 deficiency in partially ligated carotid artery (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: m6A modification is reversible and is catalyzed by a multicomponent methyltransferase complex consisting of various methyltransferases including methyltransferase like 3 (METTL3), METTL14, Wilms tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP), and KIAA1429 (Virilizer), and is erased by demethylases such as fat mass and obesity-associated protein or α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase alk B homolog 5.
source: This modification is reversible and is catalyzed by a multicomponent methyltransferase complex consisting of various methyltransferases including methyltransferase like 3 (METTL3), METTL14, Wilms tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP), and KIAA1429 (Virilizer), and is erased by demethylases such as fat mass and obesity-associated protein or α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase alk B homolog 5 (Shi et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2019 and Huang et al., 2021.

claim: m6A on mRNAs plays an important role in regulating cellular processes, including RNA stability, translation efficiency, RNA secondary structure, subcellular localization, alternative polyadenylation, and splicing.
source: As previously reported, m6A on mRNAs plays an important role in regulating cellular processes, including RNA stability, translation efﬁciency, RNA secondary structure, subcellular localization, alternative polyadenylation, and splicing (Liu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Zaccara et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Zaccara et al., 2019.

claim: METTL14 functions as the target recognition subunit by binding to RNA and then recruits METTL3 to catalyze m6A formation.
source: In the methyltransferase complex, METTL14 functions as the target recognition subunit by binding to RNA and then recruits METTL3 to catalyze m6A formation.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about the m6A methyltransferase complex.

claim: Wilms tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP) is a regulatory subunit required for the accumulation of METTL3 and METTL14 into nuclear speckles.
source: Wilms tumor 1-associated protein (WTAP) is a regulatory subunit required for the accumulation of METTL3 and METTL14 into nuclear speckles (Ping et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ping et al., 2014.

claim: KIAA1429 guides region-selective m6A methylation.
source: KIAA1429 guides region-selective m6A methylation (Yue et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yue et al., 2018.

claim: METTL3 has been demonstrated to modulate key physiological processes, including spermatogenesis, cell reprogramming, and embryonic stem cell chromatin modification.
source: As the core methyltransferase subunit, METTL3 has been demonstrated to modulate key physiological processes, including spermatogenesis (Xu et al., 2017), cell reprogramming (Chen et al., 2015), and embryonic stem cell chromatin modification (Liu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021.

claim: Atherosclerosis is the leading cause of CVD resulting in high rate of mortality in the population.
source: Atherosclerosis, resulted from endothelial dysregulation in the arterial wall (Geovanini and Libby, 2018), is the leading cause of CVD resulting in high rate of mortality in the population.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Geovanini and Libby, 2018 and draws from established knowledge.

claim: Atherosclerosis preferentially develops at branches and curvatures in the arterial tree where flow is disturbed.
source: Atherosclerosis preferentially develops at branches and curvatures in the arterial tree where flow is disturbed (Davies, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Davies, 2009.

claim: Disturbed flow pattern increases inflammatory response in ECs, including the expression of intercellular adhesion molecule 1 and vascular adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1).
source: Disturbed flow pattern increases inflammatory response in ECs, including the expression of intercellular adhesion molecule 1 and vascular adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1) (Humphrey et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Humphrey et al., 2014.

claim: Oscillatory stress (OS) could modulate atherosclerosis development by inducing the expression of DNA methyltransferases and histone modifications.
source: Recent studies have reported that oscillatory stress (OS) could modulate atherosclerosis development by inducing the expression of DNA methyltransferases (Dunn et al., 2014) and histone modifications (Hastings et al., 2007), indicating the involvement of epigenetic mechanisms in the regulation of atherogenesis.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dunn et al., 2014 and Hastings et al., 2007.

claim: TSP-1 is a shear-sensitive protein important for the regulation of vascular remodeling.
source: Numerous studies have shown that thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1, encoded by THBS1) is a shear-sensitive protein important for the regulation of vascular remodeling (Ni et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ni et al., 2010.

claim: TSP-1 can induce dysregulated blood flow, impaired vessel dilation, and increased vascular tone followed by arterial stiffening.
source: Notably, TSP-1 can induce dysregulated blood flow, impaired vessel dilation, and increased vascular tone Csányi et al., 2012 followed by arterial stiffening (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Csányi et al., 2012 and Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Thbs1 deficiency prevented lesion formation in Apoe-/- mice.
source: In addition, Thbs 1 deficiency prevented lesion formation in Apoe-/- mice (Ganguly et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ganguly et al., 2017.

claim: EGFR has been reported to be involved in vascular pathophysiology and pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in macrophages.
source: As a receptor of TSP-1, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) has been reported to be involved in vascular pathophysiology and pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in macrophages (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: EGFR-selective tyrphostin, AG1478, can reverse the phosphorylation of EGFR tyrosine-1068 induced by TSP-1 activation.
source: Moreover, EGFR-selective tyrphostin, AG1478, can reverse the phosphorylation of EGFR tyrosine-1068 induced by TSP-1 activation (Liu et al., 2009), indicating the complicated regulation between TSP-1 and EGFR with respect to vascular function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2009.

claim: Downregulation of METTL3 and hypomethylation mediate OS-induced endothelial dysfunction and atherogenesis both in vivo and in vitro.
source: Our data revealed that downregulation of METTL3 and hypomethylation mediate OS-induced endothelial dysfunction and atherogenesis both in vivo and in vitro
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The THBS1/EGFR axis is a key regulatory target of METTL3-dependent EC activation.
source: indicating that the THBS1/EGFR axis is a key regulatory target of METTL3-dependent EC activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing the relationship between METTL3, EGFR, and TSP-1.

claim: METTL3 alleviates endothelial atherogenic progression through m6A-dependent stabilization of EGFR mRNA.
source: Overall, our study revealed that METTL3 alleviates endothelial atherogenic progression through m6A-dependent stabilization of EGFR mRNA, highlighting the important role of RNA transcriptomics in atherosclerosis regulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: m6A modification plays a very important role in regulating RNA abundance.
source: As reported, m6A modification plays a very important role in regulating RNA abundance (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: EGFR ligands that specifically activate EGFR include epidermal growth factor (EGF), transforming growth factor α (TGF-α), and TSP-1.
source: EGFR ligands that specifically activate EGFR include epidermal growth factor (EGF), transforming growth factor α (TGF-α), and TSP-1 (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2009.

claim: TSP-1 is a multidomain protein that contains EGF-like repeats that indirectly activate EGFR and selected downstream signaling pathways.
source: TSP-1 is a multidomain protein that contains EGF-like repeats that indirectly activate EGFR and selected downstream signaling pathways (Garg et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Garg et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2009.

claim: TSP-1 is activated in shear-mediated arterial stiffening.
source: TSP-1 is activated in shear-mediated arterial stiffening (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: METTL3 has been reported to modulate embryonic development and spermatogenesis, and its deletion in mice causes early embryonic lethality.
source: As the core methyltransferase subunit, METTL3 has been reported to modulate embryonic development (Aguilo et al., 2015) and spermatogenesis (Xu et al., 2017), and its deletion in mice causes early embryonic lethality (Geula et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aguilo et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2017; Geula et al., 2015.

claim: METTL3 plays a central role in osteogenic differentiation and inflammatory response.
source: METTL3 also plays a central role in osteogenic differentiation and inflammatory response (Wu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019), which act similarly in ECs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: METTL3 expression is upregulated during osteoblast differentiation and downregulated after LPS stimulation.
source: METTL3 expression is upregulated during osteoblast differentiation and downregulated after LPS (lipopolysaccharide) stimulation
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about METTL3 function.

claim: METTL3 depletion enhances the expression of Smad genes and proinflammatory cytokine expression in MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways.
source: while its depletion enhances the expression of Smad genes and proinflammatory cytokine expression in MAPK and NF-κB signaling pathways (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: The development of hematopoietic stem cells (HSPCs) requires METTL3-mediated m6A modification.
source: The development of hematopoietic stem cells (HSPCs) also requires METTL3-mediated m6A modiﬁcation
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about METTL3 function in HSPCs.

claim: mettl3 deficiency in arterial endothelial cells blocks endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, followed by suppression of the generation of HSPCs through activation of Notch signaling.
source: and mettl3 deficiency in arterial endothelial cells blocks endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition, followed by suppression of the generation of HSPCs through activation of Notch signaling (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: METTL3 plays a similar role in cerebral arteriovenous malformation, and deletion of METTL3 in ECs significantly affects angiogenesis by reducing heterodimeric Notch E3 ubiquitin ligase formed by DTX1 and DTX3L.
source: METTL3 plays a similar role in cerebral arteriovenous malformation, and deletion of METTL3 in ECs significantly affects angiogenesis by reducing heterodimeric Notch E3 ubiquitin ligase formed by DTX1 and DTX3L (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: EGFR plays a role in foam cell transformation and accelerates atherosclerotic lesions characterized by accumulation of smooth muscle cells and macrophages.
source: It has been reported that EGFR plays a role in foam cell transformation and accelerates atherosclerotic lesions characterized by accumulation of smooth muscle cells and macrophages (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Explosive elevation of transcription and phosphorylation of EGFR were detected after OS treatment.
source: Although EGFR is expressed at low levels in ECs, explosive elevation of transcription and phosphorylation of EGFR were detected after OS treatment (Figure 3D and Figure 4), consistent with a report from Rizvi et al., 2013.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4, and citation to Rizvi et al., 2013.

claim: METTL3 binds to EGFR mRNA near the stop codon and is responsible for its m6A modification, modulating EGFR mRNA stability in human cancer cells.
source: METTL3 binds to EGFR mRNA near the stop codon and is responsible for its m6A modification, modulating EGFR mRNA stability in human cancer cells (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2016.

claim: EGFR is activated in response to its EGF-like repeats, such as TSP1, which require matrix metalloprotease activity, and the ligand-binding portion of the EGFR ectodomain.
source: EGFR is activated in response to its EGF-like repeats, such as TSP1, which require matrix metalloprotease activity, and the ligand-binding portion of the EGFR ectodomain (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2009.

claim: The EGFR selective tyrphostin AG1478 inhibited EGFR phosphorylation at tyrosine 1068 without affecting the total levels of EGFR and had an atheroprotective role.
source: Moreover, the EGFR selective tyrphostin AG1478 inhibited EGFR phosphorylation at tyrosine 1068 without affecting the total levels of EGFR (Garg et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2017) and had an atheroprotective role (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Garg et al., 2011 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: RNA m6A modification plays an important role in regulating endothelial activation and the atherogenesis response to oscillatory flow.
source: Our results reveal that RNA m6A modification plays an important role in regulating endothelial activation and the atherogenesis response to oscillatory flow.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: m6A modification levels were reduced concomitant with downregulation of METTL3 in atheroprone regions.
source: First, we found that m6A modification levels were reduced concomitant with downregulation of METTL3 in atheroprone regions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Oscillatory flow-derived MeRIP-seq analysis revealed that m6A modification of the EGFR 3'UTR contributes to atherogenesis.
source: Second, oscillatory flow-derived MeRIP-seq analysis revealed that m6A modification of the EGFR 3'UTR contributes to atherogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by MeRIP-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Overexpression of METTL3 restored m6A modification and reversed VCAM-1 expression and the monocyte adhesion ability response to OS.
source: Third, overexpression of METTL3 restored m6A modification and reversed VCAM-1 expression and the monocyte adhesion ability response to OS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: TSP-1/EGFR inhibition prevented the development of atherosclerosis.
source: Finally, TSP-1/EGFR inhibition prevented the development of atherosclerosis, suggesting a novel therapeutic method for atherosclerosis patients.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: METTL3 and m6A modifications could alleviate endothelial activation and atherogenesis through accelerated degradation of oscillatory flow-induced EGFR mRNA expression.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that METTL3 and m6A modifications could alleviate endothelial activation and atherogenesis through accelerated degradation of oscillatory flow-induced EGFR mRNA expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Atherosclerotic plaques tend to develop in the vasculature locations with increased shear stress and OS.
source: Atherosclerotic plaques tend to develop in the vasculature locations with increased shear stress and OS.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about atherosclerosis.

claim: EC activation in response to oscillatory flow plays important roles in regulating circulatory functions and atherosclerosis development, which is involved in the expression of various genes.
source: EC activation in response to oscillatory flow plays important roles in regulating circulatory functions and atherosclerosis development, which is involved in the expression of various genes (Li et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Li et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: m6A mRNA modification participates in a number of biological functions and in progression of ECs.
source: Recently, increasing evidence has suggested that m6A mRNA modiﬁcation participates in a number of biological functions and in progression of ECs (Shi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Xiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Xiang et al., 2017.

claim: Overexpression of Mettl3 has potential protective effects on endothelial activation in atheroprone regions.
source: Overexpression of Mettl3 has potential protective effects on endothelial activation in atheroprone regions (Figure 2F), indicating the involvement of both m6A modification and METTL3 in atherogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TSP-1 acts as a specific ligand that activates EGFR after OS treatment.
source: However, TSP-1 was not affected by METTL3 intervention, and we presume that TSP-1 acts as a specific ligand that activates EGFR after OS treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that TSP-1 is not affected by METTL3 but activates EGFR.

claim: METTL3 alleviates endothelial atherogenic progression through m6A-dependent stabilization of EGFR mRNA.
source: In summary, we provide both in vitro and in vivo evidence demonstrating that m6A RNA modification regulates progression of EC activation in response to the onset of OS and subsequently, early atherogenesis. It should be noted that METTL3-modiﬁed EGFR mRNA participates in the pathogenic mechanism of atherogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The TSP-1/EGFR axis may contribute to m6A-modified atherogenesis, and inhibition of the axis helps to retard atherosclerosis.
source: The TSP-1/EGFR axis may contribute to m6A-modified atherogenesis, and inhibition of the axis helps to retard atherosclerosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing that inhibition of TSP-1/EGFR reduces atherosclerosis.
